messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 58-year-old Latin American man married to his high school sweetheart, works as a forensic analyst in a bustling city. His world was turned upside down when he witnessed a devastating explosion at a chemical plant near his office. The event not only shook the foundations of nearby buildings but also rattled Carlos’s sense of security and competence. Since that fateful day, Carlos has become increasingly vigilant about potential dangers around him. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he feels overwhelmed by the inability to assess the risks present in these environments. This avoidance extends to his daily commute; he sticks to well-known routes and refuses to visit new coffee shops or restaurants for fear of encountering unknown hazards. His body remains constantly tense, poised as if ready to react at a moment’s notice. The explosion has also left deep scars on Carlos's self-image. He now views himself as a lousy coper, believing that his reactions since the event demonstrate his inability to handle such situations effectively. This belief is reinforced every time he finds himself jumping at sudden noises or feeling jumpy in crowded places. Even mundane tasks seem daunting now; what was once second nature has become laden with anxiety. At work, Carlos’s performance has suffered due to these fears and constant vigilance. His colleagues have noticed his avoidance of new projects and unfamiliar cases, which used to be the very things that defined him as a forensic analyst. He feels no longer capable of handling the responsibilities that once came easily, leading to self-doubt and frustration. The trauma has also reshaped Carlos’s view of the world around him. He now sees it as inherently dangerous, constantly on edge and anticipating another disaster. This pervasive sense of danger exacerbates his avoidance behaviors and his tendency to startle at sudden movements or sounds. His marriage has been strained by these changes, with his wife feeling increasingly concerned about his wellbeing. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a recent incident where he completely froze during an emergency drill at work. The simulation triggered intense panic, leaving him immobilized and shaken. This experience made Carlos realize that his fears were not only affecting his professional life but also threatening his ability to function in day-to-day situations. He is most hoping for relief from the constant tension and a return to feeling like he can handle unexpected challenges. Carlos’s current state is one of profound worry, with an overwhelming fear of losing control again in similar scenarios. His primary concern is reclaiming his sense of competence and security, both personally and professionally. He hopes that therapy will help him regain confidence in his coping abilities and reduce the constant alertness that has become a daily burden. Through this process, Carlos aims to rebuild a more balanced view of the world around him and reestablish himself as capable and resilient in the face of danger.
